title: The November meeting: what we look at before December 31
author: owen
summary: Year-end planning is a forty-minute meeting. Here is what is on the table and what to bring.
body:
Every November we meet planning clients for about forty minutes. We look at income so far, the fourth estimated payment, retirement contributions that still have room, required distributions, charitable giving and any sale that could land in either year.

Bring a recent pay stub or a profit and loss through October, your latest investment statements, and anything that will change next year: a move, a new job, a retirement date.

  • Income so far and the Q4 estimate
  • Room left in retirement plans
  • Required distributions
  • Gifts and their timing
  • Sales that could fall in either year

title: How we take documents now: no more shoeboxes on the front desk
author: nadia
summary: Clients upload to the portal, and the front desk scans anything that comes in on paper the same day.
body: For thirty years the busy season began with boxes on the front desk. Now documents go into the client portal, where each one is matched to the organizer checklist. Paper still works: drop it off and the front desk scans it the same day and hands the originals back.

title: Quarterly estimates without the guesswork
author: owen
summary: Four payments a year, sized from the year so far instead of last year's return.
body: The simplest way to set estimates is to divide last year's tax by four. It is also the most common way to end up with a large bill or a large refund. We size each payment from the year so far, two weeks before it is due.

title: The five-day close, explained
author: lena
summary: What happens in the first five business days of every month, and what lands in your inbox on day five.
body: Day one: bank and card feeds are complete. Days two and three: reconciliations. Day four: payroll, loans and adjusting entries. Day five: statements, the one-page summary and the questions list go to the owner.

title: Hiring your first employee: the payroll calendar
author: theo
summary: Registration, withholding, deposits and the four quarterly returns, laid out on one calendar.
body:
A first employee brings a state registration, withholding accounts, a deposit schedule, four quarterly returns and a January W-2. Most of it is a calendar problem, so we start by putting every date on one.

  • Register with the state employment department
  • Collect a W-4 and the state form
  • Set the deposit schedule
  • File four quarterly returns
  • Send the W-2 by January 31

title: A board treasurer's guide to the 990
author: desmond
summary: What the form asks, which parts the board should read, and why the governance pages matter.
body: The 990 is public. Donors, grant makers and reporters read it, often starting with the governance questions and the pay of the highest-paid staff. We walk boards through those pages before we file.
